title: Apex Luka Is Even More Ridiculous Than We Could’ve Imagined
text:

 We’ve long wondered what Doncic’s prime would look like. The reality is unlike anything we’ve seen before. Getty Images/Ringer illustration By Michael Pina Nov. 16, 1:26 pm UTC • 7 min Since the moment he was drafted, I’ve been dying to see what Luka Doncic’s prime would look like. 
 As a rookie, he eviscerated complex defensive schemes and established himself as a genuine basketball prodigy. Burgeoning greatness was an everyday sight. One of my most enduring memories of the bubble was Luka’s 43-point, 17-rebound, 13-assist gem that nearly broke the heavily favored Los Angeles Clippers. He was 21 years old, in the fourth playoff game of his career; Dallas won that game in overtime, tying up a series that probably should’ve been a sweep. Already, Luka was his own kind of transcendent experience—an evolutionary playmaker with unbridled confidence and zero clear offensive shortcomings. Devastating, inevitable, and endlessly clever. 
 What would he look like at the peak of his powers? A more composed Tracy McGrady with Jason Kidd’s vision? A less athletic, more technically skilled LeBron James? A world-smashing evolutionary amalgamation of Larry Bird, Magic Johnson, and Michael Jordan?
 Fast-forward to right now, when the 27-year-old savant has opened his ninth season with a heat check unlike anything anyone reading this has ever seen. Doncic is averaging a preposterous 39 points per game, which, if held, would top Jordan’s 37.1 as the highest since the merger . ( The only player in NBA history who scored more points through the first 12 games of a season is Wilt Chamberlain, in 1961 and 1962.)
 That doesn’t even tell the full story of Luka’s impact. By way of his scoring and passing, he’s directly responsible for 705 total points so far. That’s over 100 more than any other player—the same as the gap between no. 2 (Cade Cunningham) and no. 24 (Pascal Siakam). The man is in his own universe.
 Getty Images Very little of what Doncic is doing should be a surprise. He is a two-time scoring champ who’s already cracked first-team All-NBA six times, and the Lakers spent the offseason reshaping their roster with a supporting cast to complement his skill set. There’s a rim-running lob threat, 3-and-D wings, a self-starting All-Star-caliber sidekick, and a stretch big. (The Lakers are virtually unguardable when Luka shares the court with Sandro Mamukelashvili.) But that doesn’t make what Luka’s doing any less surreal. Doncic’s first quarter s yield enough thermal energy to blast a rocket through Earth’s atmosphere, and his overall numbers become half realistic when you see how he’s doing it. 
 Doncic’s true shooting percentage is 8.9 percentage points above league average . His previous high was 3.8 above league average, which happened last season. His stepback from the left wing is this generation’s sky hook—an unguardable signature move that brings individual defenders to their knees. I could post a reel of two dozen examples here, but this play against the Raptors illustrates the level of panic such a ridiculously difficult shot can cause:
 Just look at this shot chart:
 Via CourtSketch Coming into this season, Luka loved taking 3s. He had range, deceptive footwork, and enough accuracy to overwhelm opponents that were willing to switch a big on him or duck under the screen. But with so many other weapons at his disposal, Doncic didn’t overindulge behind the arc, per se. His career 3-point rate was 43 percent. 
 This year, for the first time, over half of his shots are 3s, and he’s drilling 40.8 percent of them. His 13.4 attempts and 5.5 makes per game would both be the highest marks in NBA history if the season ended today. 
 And when he’s run off the line and forced to put it on the deck, the world is his oyster. He is a master at locking his man in jail off a ball screen and forcing the opposing center to live in no-man’s-land. And when there isn’t a big man in the game, Doncic doesn’t even see who’s trying to stop him on the perimeter:
 Nobody gets to the line more than he does, either: 10.8 free throw attempts per game, with a career-best 86.6 percent of them going in. 
 Luka’s raw production is impressive, but the degree of difficulty makes it more so. Doncic’s expected field goal percentage is 38.4 percent, which ranks 127th out of 129 qualifying players. He’s outperforming that mark by 10.6 percentage points, which is second in the league behind only Stephen Curry. Some of this is because this metric doesn’t consider the difference between 3- and 2-point attempts, but, in Doncic’s case, it all checks out: The guy regularly drills some wild shots—late in the clock, hand in his face, off-balance, fading away from the basket. (Doncic is shooting 47.6 percent behind the 3-point line when there are four or fewer seconds on the shot clock. That translates to at least one liver-splitting gut punch per game.)

 Heat Check: Inside the Giannis Era’s Bumpy Start Heat Check: Inside Miami’s Bumpy Start By Logan Murdock • Nov. 12 • 10 min read Doncic already owns the highest career usage rate in both regular season and playoff history, but he’s currently flirting with the highest single-season usage rate of all time, too. If he weren’t such an elite passer—out of the pick-and-roll, of course, but Luka is also one of the more savvy and aggressive kick-ahead enthusiasts at his position —this could be construed as a bad thing. According to NBA.com, Doncic ranks first by a mile in perimeter on-ball gravity, which means that defenses blitz him a ton, particularly when he hunts a mismatch. (The only player who ranks above him in perimeter off- ball gravity is, naturally, Curry.)
 On a team that could probably use another ball handler or two— even with Austin Reaves on the court, L.A.’s offensive rating is below league average when Luka rests —Doncic’s ability to bend a defense and give his teammates an advantage attacking it is critical: 
 A whopping 20.3 percent of all his passes set up a score, whether by direct assist, hockey assist, or free throw assist. That’s the third-highest rate in the league. Pretty much all his teammates have a higher effective field goal percentage with Doncic on the court than without him: Reaves’s goes up 16.8 percent, Mamukelashvili’s goes up 13.8 percent, Matisse Thybulle’s goes up 9.4 percent, Jake LaRavia’s goes up 7.6 percent, and Collin Sexton’s goes up 14.7 percent. 
 Broadly, even with all the turnovers he commits—and there are so, so many turnovers!—the Lakers offense is a missile with Doncic in the game. They generate 130.5 points per 100 possessions (or 16.8 points above league average) when he’s on the court and just 110.6 when he sits (or 3.2 points below league average). 
 So far, his defensive limitations have mostly been masked in a hyperaggressive system that encourages ball handlers to attack Walker Kessler in the paint. Doncic has been active, handsy, and willing to sacrifice his body. The Lakers rank first in defensive turnover rate, and he’s been a legitimate reason . L.A.’s transition defense is decent when he’s on the court and much worse without him—a notable departure from most of his career leading into this season. We’ll see how long all this lasts, but it’s an encouraging start for a team that aspires to win the championship.

 Luka’s Scoring Barrage, Early-Season Apologies, and the Grizzlies’ Surprising Start Luka’s Scoring Barrage, Apologies, and the Grizzlies’ Surprising Start Luka’s Scoring, Apologies, and the Grizzlies Real Ones Real Ones • Nov. 11 • 1 hr 9 min Going back to the question that opened this column, the closest comparison to Doncic’s conceivable peak—aesthetically and statistically—was probably always going to be James Harden, who lorded over the NBA in a four-year stretch from 2017 to 2020 that included one MVP award, two seasons as the runner-up, and a third-place finish. Harden was unstoppable, a revolutionary southpaw who broke brains and forced coaches to concoct comically hopeless defensive strategies. Doncic is directly involved in so much of L.A.’s offensive game plan, but he doesn’t isolate nearly as often as Harden did . There’s more variety, tempo, and off-ball movement that gets everyone involved:
 Sets like this show why Doncic could be on the cusp of something even more grandiose and unapproachable. It’s too early to make a substantive MVP case for any one player—so much will happen between now and the end of this regular season—but this is probably the only time I can remember watching a player who could deftly notch 30 points in a game and have it feel like a letdown. 
 In the aftermath of his 2024 Finals flameout, that shocking trade, his awkward partnership with LeBron James, and the relentless criticism about his weight, temperament, and defensive shortcomings, it was easy to forget exactly how special Doncic was, let alone what his apex could still be. Too many people lost the plot. This isn’t to say we’ve already seen the best Luka has to offer, but he’s never looked more free, comfortable, or confident. Few have.
 Luka entered the NBA without training wheels. Now, as he enters a new era of his career, the rest of the league is forced to confront a constraint-free genius who’s constantly resetting the limits of what a star can and cannot accomplish. If he and everyone around him can stay healthy, beating this iteration of Doncic in a playoff series could end up being this season’s defining achievement.
